title: The study behind that claim never tested a single baby.
description:
The study behind that claim never tested a single baby. In 1993, researchers played Mozart's Sonata for Two Pianos to 36 college students, not infants.

How long the spatial reasoning boost lasted, by the original researchers' own measurement.

The study never measured IQ at all. It tested one narrow skill, folding paper and solving mazes. General intelligence was never on the test.

Governor of Georgia, who proposed $105,000 a year to give every newborn a classical music CD, then played legislators Beethoven, not Mozart, and asked if they felt smarter already.

People also did better after listening to a Stephen King story, if they enjoyed it. Researchers call it enjoyment arousal. Any music or story you like seems to work about as well as Mozart.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mozart_effect: establishes that the 1993 Nature study by Rauscher, Shaw and Ky tested 36 college students on spatial reasoning after ten minutes of Mozart's Sonata for Two Pianos K.448, found the boost lasted no longer than the fifteen minute testing window, and that the study never measured general IQ at all; also records Georgia governor Zell Miller's 13 January 1998 budget proposal of $105,000 a year for a classical music tape or CD for every newborn, his quote asking legislators if they felt smarter after he played them Beethoven's Ode to Joy, and Christopher Chabris's 1999 Nature meta analysis finding the effect was small and driven by what he called enjoyment arousal, illustrated by a study where a Stephen King story produced the same spatial boost as Mozart for listeners who enjoyed it.
- https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8684937/: an independent experimental test of the Mozart effect that failed to reproduce the original spatial reasoning boost.
